announcements.title: November 2026 Release: Governance for AI Agents
announcements.summary: Govern how AI agents work in your testing. November brings model constraints, agent access controls, token limits, AI auditing, GitLab support in AI Test Creation, and a new timeline view.
announcements.body:
Testkube November 2026 release is live

This month is about governance for AI agents. If you have been waiting for the controls before letting agents loose on your testing, they are here.

Governance for AI agents
Four new controls, all under a new AI Governance area in org settings:

  • Model constraints: limit which models an agent (or a member) may use
  • Agent access: make an agent private while you build it, limit it by role, or assign it to a resource group
  • Token limits: cap what a member, agent, environment or org can spend per hour, week or month. The first limit reached blocks further use until the window resets. Works with models that report token usage.
  • AI auditing: filter the audit log to MCP tool calls, export as JSON, and send AI session traces to CloudWatch or any OTLP endpoint via OpenTelemetry

New chats are also private by default now. You can make one public, but not the other way round.

GitLab support
AI Test Creation and the advanced Git integration now work with GitLab as well as GitHub, including running tests when a merge request opens.

Your agents inside test creation
Test creation sessions can now use the AI agents you have defined. Pull a requirement from your tracker and refine a test against it, or take an action in another tool as part of the session. Any tool with an MCP server can take part.

Timeline view
A new view of executions over time, with CPU and memory consumption plotted above it and a per-Runner breakdown. Real time, full screen, shareable by link.

Also

  • Search across all logs of an execution from one view
  • A clearer review and push flow in AI Test Creation

Full details in Ole’s post: November 2026 Release: Governance for AI Agents

announcements.title: October 2026 Release: Sort and Route Failed Tests
announcements.summary: Know why a test failed before you open a log. October brings failure categories, webhook routing by failure type, dependency caching, and AI Test Creation for on-prem.
announcements.body:
Release Alert! 🚀

Hello wonderful humans! The October 2026 release is live! Here’s what’s new:

🔍 See what kind of failures you are dealing with:
Failure categories now show up in the executions list, so you can tell without opening the logs. Filter by failure type or route notifications to different places—for example, infrastructure failures to one Slack channel and test failures to another. See the failure categories.

🤖 AI Test Creation is now available on-prem
Describe a test in plain language, and Testkube generates it, runs it in your environment, and opens a pull request with the result. More on AI Test Creation.

💥 Less clicking for admins
We’ve reworked organization-level user and permission management to make finding users, changing permissions, and making bulk updates easier. (video demo here)

Cache dependencies between runs
Reuse dependencies and other intermediate output across executions, with configurable cache keys and expiration times. Caching docs.

A few more additions:

  • Testkube for GitHub: see Testkube results directly in GitHub with our new Chrome extension. Install it here.
  • Audit logs: search by resource name or ID to find related actions.
  • Agent → Runner: the component that runs your tests is now called the Runner, to avoid confusion with AI Agents. Existing agent commands still work. Details.
  • JUnit reports: link directly to a specific test case in a report.
